blocks.content: Now that you know TCP numbers every single byte precisely, from the sequence numbers topic, the natural next question is how the receiver actually uses those numbers to tell the sender what it has successfully received. That is exactly what the acknowledgment number field does, and this topic covers exactly how.

Getting this one mechanism right explains a surprising amount of TCP behavior at once, including how it stays efficient even while confirming huge amounts of data, and how it deals cleanly with a genuine gap in the middle of the stream.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437216344-403489106.png
1. The Single Most Important Detail: Acknowledgments Are Cumulative
blocks.text: 1. The Single Most Important Detail: Acknowledgments Are Cumulative

blocks.content: An acknowledgment number in TCP does not simply say, I received byte X. It says specifically, I have successfully received everything UP TO byte X, and I am now expecting byte X next. This cumulative nature is a genuinely important detail that trips people up if it gets missed.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437216345-813756651.png
blocks.alt: The Single Most Important Detail: Acknowledgments Are Cumulative

blocks.title: State it precisely
blocks.content: An acknowledgment number is not a pointer to one specific byte you received, it is a running confirmation of everything received so far, in order, without a single gap.
2. A Worked Example Making This Concrete
blocks.text: 2. A Worked Example Making This Concrete

blocks.content: A receiver has successfully gotten bytes 1000 through 1799 in order. It sends back an acknowledgment number of 1800, meaning specifically: I have everything up through 1799, send me 1800 next. Not simply, I got something around byte 1800.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437216346-871487904.png
blocks.alt: A Worked Example Making This Concrete

blocks.content: 3. Why Cumulative, Rather Than Acknowledging Each Piece Separately
blocks.text: 3. Why Cumulative, Rather Than Acknowledging Each Piece Separately

blocks.content: Cumulative acknowledgment is efficient. One single acknowledgment number can confirm a large amount of received data at once. There is no need to send a separate acknowledgment for every individual byte or segment, the receiver just needs to report the single highest point up to which everything has arrived correctly and in order.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437216346-45122864.png
blocks.alt: Why Cumulative, Rather Than Acknowledging Each Piece Separately

blocks.content: 4. The Critical Detail: A Gap Freezes the Acknowledgment Number
blocks.text: 4. The Critical Detail: A Gap Freezes the Acknowledgment Number

blocks.content: If bytes 1000 to 1499 arrive, then bytes 2000 to 2499 arrive out of order, skipping ahead, before bytes 1500 to 1999 have arrived at all, the acknowledgment number STAYS at 1500, not 2500. There is still a genuine gap in the middle. Cumulative acknowledgment specifically cannot skip over a hole, it can only advance once every byte up to that point has actually arrived.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437216823-597605502.png
blocks.alt: The Critical Detail: A Gap Freezes the Acknowledgment Number

5. Piggybacking: A Practical Efficiency Detail

In a connection where both sides are actively sending data to each other, an acknowledgment does not need to be sent as its own separate, empty segment. It can be piggybacked onto a normal data segment already being sent in the other direction, saving real overhead by combining two jobs into one segment.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437216824-38454.png
6. Duplicate Acknowledgments: A Meaningful Signal

If the receiver keeps getting new data but a specific gap never gets filled, it will keep sending the SAME acknowledgment number over and over, repeating, I am still waiting for that missing byte. Receiving several of these identical, duplicate acknowledgments in a row is actually a meaningful signal to the sender that something specific is genuinely missing, covered in full in the dedicated retransmission topic next in this module.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437216824-104701460.png
7. Delayed Acknowledgment: A Real World Optimization
blocks.text: 7. Delayed Acknowledgment: A Real World Optimization

blocks.content: Rather than acknowledging literally every single segment the instant it arrives, many real TCP implementations deliberately wait a short moment, hoping to either piggyback the acknowledgment on outgoing data or combine several arriving segments into one acknowledgment, trading a small amount of delay for meaningfully less acknowledgment traffic overall.

blocks.title: A small delay in exchange for less overhead
blocks.content: This is a deliberate design tradeoff, not a bug or a slowdown. A brief, bounded wait before acknowledging often lets several confirmations merge into one, genuinely reducing overall traffic on the connection.
8. Every Segment Separately Versus Cumulative Acknowledgment
blocks.text: 8. Every Segment Separately Versus Cumulative Acknowledgment

Think of a mail carrier confirming, I have delivered everything up through package number 47, rather than separately confirming receipt of every single individual package one at a time. One clear confirmation covers everything received so far in one shot.

blocks.content: 9. Common Mistakes and Key Takeaways

["Assuming an acknowledgment number confirms only one specific byte or segment, when it actually confirms everything up to and including that point cumulatively.","Assuming acknowledgment numbers can skip ahead over a genuine gap in the data, when cumulative acknowledgment specifically cannot do that.","An acknowledgment number means everything up to that point has arrived, not just that one specific byte.","A gap in the middle of the stream freezes the acknowledgment number until it is filled.","Piggybacking and delayed acknowledgment are real efficiency optimizations, not shortcuts that break correctness.","Repeated identical acknowledgments are a meaningful early signal of loss."]
items: Assuming an acknowledgment number confirms only one specific byte or segment, when it actually confirms everything up to and including that point cumulatively.
Assuming acknowledgment numbers can skip ahead over a genuine gap in the data, when cumulative acknowledgment specifically cannot do that.
An acknowledgment number means everything up to that point has arrived, not just that one specific byte.
A gap in the middle of the stream freezes the acknowledgment number until it is filled.
Piggybacking and delayed acknowledgment are real efficiency optimizations, not shortcuts that break correctness.
Repeated identical acknowledgments are a meaningful early signal of loss.
